steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the run-state migration section of an encyclopedia article on ARM big.LITTLE, explaining the different ways the big and LITTLE cores can be arranged and scheduled, with example chips.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Three ways to arrange the cores
- Clustered switching
- In-kernel switcher (CPU migration)
- Heterogeneous multi-processing (global task scheduling)

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Intro
  - three arrangements; depends on SoC layout and kernel scheduler
- Clustered switching
  - first, simplest; identically sized clusters of "big" or "LITTLE" cores
  - OS scheduler sees one cluster at a time; load low <-> high -> switch to other cluster
  - data passed through common L2 cache; active cluster powered off, other activated
  - Cache Coherent Interconnect (CCI)
  - Samsung Exynos 5 Octa (5410)
- In-kernel switcher (IKS)
  - pair "big" core with "LITTLE" core, possibly many identical pairs per chip
  - each pair = virtual core; only one real core (fully) powered up at a time
  - big for high demand, LITTLE for low
  - demand changes: incoming core powered up, running state transferred, outgoing shut down, continue on new core
  - via cpufreq framework; complete IKS in Linux 3.11
  - improvement over cluster migration; each pair visible to scheduler
  - non-symmetric grouping: one or two big + many LITTLE, or vice versa
  - Nvidia Tegra 3 low-power "companion core" similar
- HMP (global task scheduling)
  - most powerful; all physical cores at once
  - high priority / compute-heavy threads -> big; low priority, background -> LITTLE
  - no need for matching numbers of big and LITTLE
  - Samsung Exynos from Exynos 5 Octa series (5420, 5422, 5430); Apple A series from A11; hexa-core Rockchip RK3399

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
There are three ways to arrange the different processor cores in a big.LITTLE design. Which one is used depends on the actual SoC layout and on the scheduler that is implemented in the kernel.

### Clustered switching

The clustered model is the first implementation and also the simplest one. The processor is arranged into clusters of "big" or "LITTLE" cores, and the clusters are the same size. The operating system scheduler can only see one cluster at a time. When the load on the whole processor changes between low and high, the system switches over to the other cluster. Then all the relevant data are passed through the common L2 cache, and the active core cluster is powered off and the other one is activated. A Cache Coherent Interconnect (CCI) is used. This model was implemented in the Samsung Exynos 5 Octa (5410).

### In-kernel switcher (CPU migration)

- big + LITTLE core in pairs, maybe many identical pairs per chip; each pair a virtual core, only one real core (fully) powered at a time
- big when demand high, LITTLE when low; on change: power up incoming, transfer running state, shut down outgoing, continue on new core
- cpufreq framework; complete IKS in Linux 3.11; improvement over cluster migration, each pair visible to scheduler
- non-symmetric grouping: one or two big + many LITTLE, or vice versa; Nvidia Tegra 3 "companion core"

### Heterogeneous multi-processing (global task scheduling)

- most powerful; all physical cores at the same time
- high priority / computationally intense threads on big; less priority, background tasks on LITTLE
- no matching numbers needed
- Samsung Exynos from Exynos 5 Octa series (5420, 5422, 5430); Apple A series from A11; hexa-core Rockchip RK3399

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
There are three ways to arrange the different processor cores in a big.LITTLE design. Which one is used depends on the actual SoC layout and on the scheduler that is implemented in the kernel.

### Clustered switching

The clustered model is the first implementation and also the simplest one. The processor is arranged into clusters of "big" or "LITTLE" cores, and the clusters are the same size. The operating system scheduler can only see one cluster at a time. When the load on the whole processor changes between low and high, the system switches over to the other cluster. Then all the relevant data are passed through the common L2 cache, and the active core cluster is powered off and the other one is activated. A Cache Coherent Interconnect (CCI) is used. This model was implemented in the Samsung Exynos 5 Octa (5410).

### In-kernel switcher (CPU migration)

CPU migration with the in-kernel switcher (IKS) means pairing up a "big" core with a "LITTLE" core, and there can be many identical pairs in one chip. Each pair works as one virtual core, as it is called, and only one real core is (fully) powered up and running at a time. When demand is high the "big" core is used and when demand is low the "LITTLE" core is used. When the demand on the virtual core changes (between high and low), the incoming core is powered up, the running state is transferred, the outgoing core is shut down, and then processing continues on the new core. The switching is done with the cpufreq framework. A complete big.LITTLE IKS implementation was added in Linux 3.11. big.LITTLE IKS improves on cluster migration, and the main difference is that each pair is visible to the scheduler.

There is also a more complex arrangement where the "big" and "LITTLE" cores are grouped non-symmetrically. One chip could have one or two "big" cores and a lot more "LITTLE" cores, or the other way around. Nvidia made something similar to this with the low-power "companion core" in its Tegra 3 System-on-Chip.

### Heterogeneous multi-processing (global task scheduling)

Heterogeneous multi-processing (HMP) is the most powerful use model of the big.LITTLE architecture, and it lets all the physical cores be used at the same time. In this case threads that have high priority or high computational intensity can be put on the "big" cores, and threads with less priority or less computational intensity, like background tasks, can be run on the "LITTLE" cores. This model also does not need the numbers of "big" and "LITTLE" cores to match.

This model was implemented in the Samsung Exynos starting with the Exynos 5 Octa series (5420, 5422, 5430), and in Apple A series processors starting with the Apple A11. The hexa-core Rockchip RK3399 SoC is another example.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
There are three ways[1] for the different processor cores to be arranged in a big.LITTLE design, depending on the actual SoC layout and the scheduler implemented in the kernel.[2]

### Clustered switching

The clustered model is the first and simplest implementation, arranging the processor into identically sized clusters of "big" or "LITTLE" cores. The operating system scheduler can only see one cluster at a time; when the load on the whole processor changes between low and high, the system switches to the other cluster. All relevant data are then passed through the common L2 cache, the active core cluster is powered off and the other one is activated. A Cache Coherent Interconnect (CCI) is used. This model was implemented in the Samsung Exynos 5 Octa (5410).[3]

### In-kernel switcher (CPU migration)

CPU migration via the in-kernel switcher (IKS) pairs up a "big" core with a "LITTLE" core, possibly with many identical pairs in one chip. Each pair operates as one so-called virtual core, and only one real core is (fully) powered up and running at a time. The "big" core is used when demand is high and the "LITTLE" core when demand is low. When demand on the virtual core changes (between high and low), the incoming core is powered up, running state is transferred, the outgoing core is shut down, and processing continues on the new core. Switching is done via the cpufreq framework. A complete big.LITTLE IKS implementation was added in Linux 3.11. big.LITTLE IKS is an improvement on cluster migration, the main difference being that each pair is visible to the scheduler.

A more complex arrangement involves a non-symmetric grouping of "big" and "LITTLE" cores. A single chip could have one or two "big" cores and many more "LITTLE" cores, or vice versa. Nvidia created something similar with the low-power "companion core" in its Tegra 3 System-on-Chip.

### Heterogeneous multi-processing (global task scheduling)

The most powerful use model of the big.LITTLE architecture is heterogeneous multi-processing (HMP), which allows all physical cores to be used at the same time. In this case, threads with high priority or computational intensity can be allocated to the "big" cores, while threads with less priority or less computational intensity, such as background tasks, can be handled by the "LITTLE" cores.[4] This model also does not require matching numbers of "big" and "LITTLE" cores.

This model has been implemented in the Samsung Exynos starting with the Exynos 5 Octa series (5420, 5422, 5430),[5,6] and in Apple A series processors starting with the Apple A11.[7] Another example is the hexa-core Rockchip RK3399 SoC.
